content: Fetuins are a group of blood proteins synthesized in the liver and subsequently released into the bloodstream. They belong to a broad category of binding proteins that facilitate the transport and bioavailability of various substances within the circulatory system. Among these, fetuin-A serves as a primary carrier protein for free fatty acids in the bloodstream. The most well-known carrier protein in the blood is serum albumin, which is the most abundant protein in the plasma of adult animals. However, fetuin is more prevalent in fetal blood, which is the origin of its name, derived from the Latin word fetus. For instance, fetal bovine serum contains higher levels of fetuin compared to albumin, whereas adult serum exhibits the opposite pattern, with albumin being more abundant than fetuin. In humans, fetuin is also referred to as α2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG), α2-HS, A2HS, AHS, HSGA, or fetuin-A. The gene encoding fetuin-A exists as a single-copy gene in both human and mouse genomes. Another closely related gene, fetuin-B, is also present in the genomes of humans, rats, and mice. Like fetuin-A, fetuin-B is primarily produced in the liver, although it is also synthesized to a lesser extent by other secretory tissues. Fetuins are found across all vertebrate genomes, including those of fish and reptiles. These proteins belong to the cystatin superfamily, having evolved from the cystatin protein through gene duplication and segment exchange. Other members of this superfamily include histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG) and kininogen (KNG). The physiological role of fetuin-A has been extensively studied using gene knockout models in mice. Mice lacking the fetuin-A gene are completely deficient in this protein. When these fetuin-A-deficient mice were fed a diet rich in minerals, they developed widespread calcification (ectopic mineralization) in organs such as the lungs, heart, and kidneys. This calcification was significantly exacerbated when the fetuin-A knockout was combined with the DBA/2 genetic background, a mouse strain known for its susceptibility to dystrophic calcification, a process in which damaged tissues undergo mineralization. In these mice, the absence of fetuin-A led to spontaneous, systemic calcification even in the absence of a mineral-rich diet or tissue trauma. Consequently, fetuin-A is considered a potent inhibitor of systemic calcification. Additionally, free fatty acids have been shown to upregulate fetuin-A expression by activating the pro-inflammatory protein NF-κB. Fetuin-A facilitates the binding of free fatty acids to TLR4 receptors, which in turn induces insulin resistance in mice. Fetuin-A was first identified as an inhibitor of vascular calcification in the early 1990s. Since then, its biological roles have been increasingly recognized. It has been shown to play a critical role in the development of insulin resistance in the liver induced by free fatty acids. Elevated levels of fetuin-A in individuals with pre-diabetes are associated with a higher likelihood of progression to diabetes and a reduced likelihood of returning to normal blood sugar levels. Thus, fetuin-A serves as a predictor of adverse glycemic outcomes in pre-diabetes. Obese individuals exhibit increased circulating levels of fetuin-A, which can be reduced through interventions such as metformin treatment, exercise, or weight loss. Elevated fetuin-A levels have also been linked to a higher incidence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and cardiovascular events, likely due to its pro-inflammatory effects. Paradoxically, fetuin-A also exhibits anti-inflammatory properties. It acts as a negative acute-phase reactant during sepsis and endotoxemia, promotes wound healing, and provides neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease. Conversely, reduced levels of fetuin-A are associated with increased disease activity in conditions such as obstructive lung disease, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. These seemingly contradictory effects may be explained by the differential interactions of fetuin-A with various toll-like receptors (TLRs) in different tissues and organ systems.
